warmup.q: A Netty server runs 2 worker event loops: two threads that each serve a share of the connections. Six clients connect. The handler for client 3 calls a database the blocking way, and the call takes 500 ms. Which clients notice?
options: The clients that share client 3's event loop, roughly half of them
All six clients, because Netty serializes the whole server
None of them: Netty runs each read on a fresh thread
warmup.why: Netty gives each new channel to one loop of the group, in turn, and keeps it there for life, like a clerk who keeps the same row of boxes. Every handler call for those channels runs on that loop's one thread. Clients 1, 3 and 5 share a loop, so 1 and 5 wait behind client 3's query. The clients on the other loop never notice.

opening:
Our post office has outgrown its single clerk, so it hires a team. Each clerk gets a row of boxes in the wall and keeps it for good. Letters from those boxes pass along a line of stations: one cuts the stream of pages into whole letters, one reads the handwriting, one writes the answer. Replies travel back through a packing station. One house rule matters more than the rest: a clerk never stops to make a phone call, because every box in the row waits while the clerk is on the phone.

That post office is Netty, a Java library for network servers and clients, and the base under Vert.x (lesson 5) and many other tools. It's the select loop from NIO: buffers, channels and selectors, written once and written well. The trap is that it makes waiting look harmless. A handler that waits "only a few milliseconds" passes its tests, then stalls hundreds of connections at once.

In this lesson, we'll start a Netty server, see which thread serves each connection, follow a line through the pipeline, and break the house rule on purpose. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a team of clerks, each with a row of boxes, a line of stations and one house rule. Netty names them: an event loop owns its channels for life, a pipeline carries reads in and writes out, and a handler that waits stalls every channel on its loop.

Now search your own handlers, or any callback that runs on an event loop, for a call that waits: a database query, Thread.sleep, future.get(). Each one is a phone call on the clerk's time.

Next, we'll put Netty to work on real bytes. How does a pipeline cut a byte stream into whole messages, who hands each buffer back, and what stops a slow client from filling your memory?

sections.h: One clerk per row of boxes: the event loop and its group
sections.html:
Netty keeps the shape of the select loop we wrote by hand. Each piece from the last lesson has a Netty name, and each one fixes something we had to get right ourselves:

Our loop in lesson 2 Netty What it fixes
one thread running select() EventLoop, several in an EventLoopGroup one loop per core instead of one per server
the Conn card on each key Channel and its ChannelPipeline of handlers per-connection state and logic in small pieces
flip() and compact() by hand ByteBuf, with separate read and write indexes no mode to get wrong (lesson 4)
pending bytes and arming OP_WRITE the channel's outbound buffer Netty sets and clears OP_WRITE for you
dropping OP_READ when full auto-read and writability backpressure as a setting (lesson 4)
nothing: only the loop could touch its keys a task queue on every loop any thread can hand the loop work safely

A few names first. A channel is Netty's object for one connection, with its socket (its end of the network connection) and its handlers. A handler is a small object that reacts to that connection's events, such as "a message arrived". An event loop is one thread that runs a selector (the JDK object from lesson 2 that reports which connections are ready) over many channels, plus a queue of tasks that other threads can hand it. It's the clerk, the row of boxes, and the clerk's in-tray. An event loop group is the team of clerks.

Our running example in this lesson is the post office's price desk. A client sends a line describing a letter or a parcel, and the server answers with a line of its own. In Netty 4.2 you build each group by naming its IO handler, the part that talks to the operating system:

Java
EventLoopGroup boss = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory());   // accepts connections
EventLoopGroup workers = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory());  // serves them
Channel server = new ServerBootstrap()
        .group(boss, workers)
        .channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class)
        .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() {
            @Override
            protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) {
                ch.pipeline().addLast(new LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), new StringDecoder(UTF_8),
                        new StringEncoder(UTF_8), new QuoteHandler());
            }
        })
        .bind(8080).sync().channel();
Kotlin
val boss = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory())     // accepts connections
val workers = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory())    // serves them
val server = ServerBootstrap()
    .group(boss, workers)
    .channel(NioServerSocketChannel::class.java)
    .childHandler(object : ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() {
        override fun initChannel(ch: SocketChannel) {
            ch.pipeline().addLast(LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), StringDecoder(UTF_8),
                StringEncoder(UTF_8), QuoteHandler())
        }
    })
    .bind(8080).sync().channel()

The boss group only accepts connections and hands each one to a worker loop, so one boss thread is plenty for one port. ServerBootstrap, Netty's helper for starting a server, wires the rest: which groups, which kind of channel, and a ChannelInitializer that sets up the stations for each new connection. We'll walk those stations in the next section.

If you learned Netty 4.1, you wrote new NioEventLoopGroup(). Netty 4.2 deprecated it, along with its epoll and kqueue cousins. Ask the compiler (javac -Xlint:deprecation), and it says so without hesitation: warning: [deprecation] NioEventLoopGroup in io.netty.channel.nio has been deprecated. The replacement is always MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup plus a factory: NioIoHandler, EpollIoHandler, KQueueIoHandler or IoUringIoHandler. The bootstrap still names the matching channel class.

Small servers often pass one group to .group(group), so the same loops accept and serve. The lab does that, with a single loop, so you can watch a blocked loop clearly.

Without a thread count, a group gets two loops per core. EventLoopDemo, in the Try it below, prints 8 on a 4-core machine. Then it connects four clients, one after another, to a group of two worker loops. One run printed (the bytes from lines left out):

default loop count: 8 (availableProcessors=4)
client port 46484 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-1, inEventLoop=true
client port 46488 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-2, inEventLoop=true
client port 46490 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-1, inEventLoop=true
client port 46498 registered on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-2, inEventLoop=true

Each new connection is registered with one loop, in turn, and stays there for life. That lifelong seat is why Netty handlers rarely need locks: every event for a channel runs on its loop's one thread, one after another. It's also why one slow handler hurts. Every other channel on that loop waits behind it, like every box in a row waiting for its one clerk.

A channel belongs to one event loop for life. Its handlers never run at once, and they share the loop's one thread.

A clerk with a row of boxes still needs a way to handle each letter. That's the pipeline.

try.title: See which loop owns each connection
steps: Open EventLoopDemo.java (or EventLoopDemo.kt). It starts a server with one accepting loop and two worker loops, then connects four clients one after another.
Predict the thread name for the third and fourth client, and what inEventLoop() returns inside the handler.
Run it. Then change the worker group to new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, ...) and run it again.

code.title: EventLoopDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l03; import io.netty.bootstrap.ServerBootstrap; import io.netty.channel.Channel; import io.netty.channel.ChannelHandlerContext; import io.netty.channel.ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter; import io.netty.channel.ChannelInitializer; import io.netty.channel.EventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.nio.NioIoHandler; import io.netty.channel.socket.SocketChannel; import io.netty.channel.socket.nio.NioServerSocketChannel; import java.io.InputStream; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.net.Socket; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Which event-loop thread serves each connection? One acceptor loop, two worker loops, four clients. */ public class EventLoopDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup defaults = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory()); System.out.println("default loop count: " + defaults.executorCount() + " (availableProcessors=" + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + ")"); defaults.shutdownGracefully(0, 0, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync(); EventLoopGroup boss = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); // accepts EventLoopGroup workers = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(2, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); // serves try { Channel server = new ServerBootstrap() .group(boss, workers) .channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class) .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { @Override protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) { ch.pipeline().addLast(new ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter() { @Override public void channelActive(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { System.out.printf("client port %d registered on %s, inEventLoop=%s%n", ((InetSocketAddress) ctx.channel().remoteAddress()).getPort(), Thread.currentThread().getName(), ctx.channel().eventLoop().inEventLoop()); } @Override public void channelRead(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Object msg) { System.out.printf(" bytes from port %d handled on %s%n", ((InetSocketAddress) ctx.channel().remoteAddress()).getPort(), Thread.currentThread().getName()); ctx.writeAndFlush(msg); // echo: the write takes ownership of msg, no release here } }); } }) .bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0).sync().channel(); int port = ((InetSocketAddress) server.localAddress()).getPort(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { try (Socket client = new Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port)) { client.getOutputStream().write("hi".getBytes()); InputStream in = client.getInputStream(); in.readNBytes(2); } } server.close().sync(); } finally { boss.shutdownGracefully(0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync(); workers.shutdownGracefully(0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync(); } } }

try.expect: The default group reports 8 loops on a 4-core machine. The four clients alternate between multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-4-1 and -4-2, and each client's bytes are handled on the same thread that registered it, with inEventLoop=true. With one worker loop, all four land on the same thread: one clerk, the whole wall.

sections.h: The sorting line: reads flow in, writes flow out
sections.html:
Every channel has a ChannelPipeline: a list of handlers between a head, next to the socket, and a tail. It's the line of stations each letter passes. Two kinds of traffic move along it, in opposite directions.

Each handler gets a ChannelHandlerContext, usually called ctx. It's the handler's own place on the line, with methods to pass an event to the next station or to start a write from there.

Inbound events start at the head and move toward the tail. The main ones are channelActive when the connection opens, channelRead for each message, channelReadComplete after a batch of reads, and exceptionCaught when something fails. Inbound handlers change the message on its way. At the price desk, LineBasedFrameDecoder turns the stream of bytes into one ByteBuf (Netty's buffer, lesson 4) per line, and StringDecoder turns that into a String. The last handler only ever sees whole lines.

Outbound operations go the other way. write, flush and close start where you call them and move toward the head. StringEncoder sits on that path and turns your String back into bytes. So the order of addLast is the order inbound events see the handlers, and the reverse of the order writes see them.

One detail decides which handlers a write passes. ctx.writeAndFlush(msg) starts at the current handler and goes toward the head, skipping everything after it. ctx.channel().writeAndFlush(msg) starts at the tail and passes every outbound handler. Inside a handler, use ctx unless you really want the whole line.

PipelineDemo puts taps between the stations, handlers that print whatever passes, and feeds two lines in three pieces. Its last handler is the shout-back desk: it answers each line in upper case.

writeInbound("hel")
writeInbound("lo\nwor")
   in,  after framing : ByteBuf "hello"
   in,  business sees : String "hello"
   out, to the wire   : ByteBuf "HELLO\n"
writeInbound("ld\n")
   ...
100-byte line -> TooLongFrameException: frame length (100) exceeds the allowed maximum (64)
finish() = false

The first piece produced nothing. The decoder kept the bytes and waited for the end of the line: last lesson's framing problem, solved once on the line. The 64-byte limit matters as much. Without it, a client that never sends a newline makes the decoder keep its bytes forever. With it, the 100-byte line fails at once.

Here the post office picture breaks. On a real sorting line, each station has its own worker, and they all work at the same time. In Netty, one clerk carries each letter through every station, start to finish, before picking up the next. That's exactly why one slow station stops the whole row.

The demo runs on an EmbeddedChannel, a channel with no socket and no real event loop. writeInbound pushes bytes in at the head, readOutbound returns what reached the head on the way out, and finish() says whether anything was left over. It's the fastest way to test a handler, and this lesson's lab uses it.

Reads flow from head to tail, and writes flow from where you start them toward the head. The order of addLast decides what each handler sees.

Every one of those stations runs on the clerk's one thread. So what happens when a station has to wait?

try.title: Move the tap past the encoder
steps: Run PipelineDemo (or PipelineDemoKt) and match each printed line to a station in the figure.

code.title: PipelineDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l03; import io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf; import io.netty.buffer.Unpooled; import io.netty.channel.ChannelHandlerContext; import io.netty.channel.ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter; import io.netty.channel.ChannelOutboundHandlerAdapter; import io.netty.channel.ChannelPromise; import io.netty.channel.SimpleChannelInboundHandler; import io.netty.channel.embedded.EmbeddedChannel; import io.netty.handler.codec.LineBasedFrameDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringEncoder; import java.util.List; import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8; /** Feeds bytes into a pipeline in fragments and prints what each stage sees, inbound and outbound. */ public class PipelineDemo { static String describe(Object msg) { String text = msg instanceof ByteBuf b ? b.toString(UTF_8) : msg.toString(); String type = msg instanceof ByteBuf ? "ByteBuf" : msg.getClass().getSimpleName(); return type + " \"" + text.replace("\n", "\\n") + "\""; } public static void main(String[] args) { EmbeddedChannel ch = new EmbeddedChannel( new LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), // inbound: bytes -> one ByteBuf per line new ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter() { // inbound tap @Override public void channelRead(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Object msg) { System.out.println(" in, after framing : " + describe(msg)); ctx.fireChannelRead(msg); // pass it on (ownership moves with it) } }, new StringDecoder(UTF_8), // inbound: ByteBuf -> String new ChannelOutboundHandlerAdapter() { // outbound tap, nearer the head than the encoder @Override public void write(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Object msg, ChannelPromise promise) { System.out.println(" out, to the wire : " + describe(msg)); ctx.write(msg, promise); } }, new StringEncoder(UTF_8), // outbound: String -> ByteBuf new SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>() { // business logic, last @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { System.out.println(" in, business sees : String \"" + line + "\""); ctx.writeAndFlush(line.toUpperCase() + "\n"); // travels toward the head } }); for (String fragment : List.of("hel", "lo\nwor", "ld\n")) { System.out.println("writeInbound(\"" + fragment.replace("\n", "\\n") + "\")"); ch.writeInbound(Unpooled.copiedBuffer(fragment, UTF_8)); ByteBuf out; while ((out = ch.readOutbound()) != null) out.release(); } try { ch.writeInbound(Unpooled.copiedBuffer("x".repeat(100) + "\n", UTF_8)); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println("100-byte line -> " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("finish() = " + ch.finish()); } }

Writes travel from the business handler toward the head, so a handler's place on the line decides what it sees.

video.title: Netty's event loop and pipeline: reads flow in, writes flow out, never block

sections.h: The golden rule: the clerk never makes a phone call
sections.html:
Handlers run on the event loop's thread. A handler that sleeps, waits for a lock, or calls a database the blocking way holds that thread, and every other channel on the loop waits with it. That's the golden rule of event loops: never block the loop. In the post office, it's the clerk who stops to phone the back office about a price while the whole row of boxes fills up.

BlockingLoopDemo breaks the rule on purpose, with one event loop and two clients. Client A asks for SLOW, which sleeps 1 s to stand in for a slow call. Client B asks for FAST 50 ms later. FAST needs no work, so it should come back in a few milliseconds. One run on a busy 4-core machine printed:

[blocking in the handler]
   event-loop lag probe: 995 ms
   FAST reply after 996 ms: FAST on multiThreadIoEventLoopGroup-2-1
[dispatch to the back office]
   event-loop lag probe: 0 ms
   FAST reply after 3 ms: FAST on back-office

With the handler blocking, FAST took 996 ms: it waited for the clerk to hang up. With the slow part handed off, it took 3 ms.

The lag probe in that output is a trick worth keeping. Slip an empty task into the loop's in-tray and time how long it waits to run. On a healthy loop, it's close to 0.

Netty 4.1 offered a shortcut: pipeline.addLast(executorGroup, "name", handler) ran one handler on a separate group of threads. Netty 4.2 deprecated those versions of addLast, and compiling the old call prints warning: [deprecation] addLast(EventExecutorGroup,String,ChannelHandler) in ChannelPipeline has been deprecated. The commit that did it (d64340b) says per-handler executors caused more problems than they solved, and that it's "much better to dispatch it manually".

Manual dispatch is three lines. Hand the slow part to a pool of your own, the back office, and write the reply from there:

Java
@Override
protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) {
    backOffice.execute(() -> {                     // 1. leave the event loop
        String quote = priceBook.lookup(line);     // 2. wait here: a database, a slow web service
        ctx.writeAndFlush(quote + "\n");           // 3. safe from any thread
    });
}
Kotlin
override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) {
    backOffice.execute {                           // 1. leave the event loop
        val quote = priceBook.lookup(line)         // 2. wait here: a database, a slow web service
        ctx.writeAndFlush("$quote\n")              // 3. safe from any thread
    }
}

Step 3 works because Netty asks inEventLoop(), "am I on this channel's loop?", on every write. Called from another thread, the write becomes a task in the channel's own in-tray, so the pipeline still runs on one thread. If code in the pool needs the handler's own fields, hop back first with ctx.executor().execute(...), so that state stays with the clerk. Size the back office like any blocking pool: with Little's law and the limits of the service you call, from lesson 1, or with virtual threads.

The event loop serves everyone, so it must never wait for anyone. Hand the waiting to another thread.

The threading rules are the heart of Netty, and 4.2 left them alone. A few other things did change.

code.html: package workbench.nio.l03; import io.netty.bootstrap.ServerBootstrap; import io.netty.channel.Channel; import io.netty.channel.ChannelHandlerContext; import io.netty.channel.ChannelInitializer; import io.netty.channel.EventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.SimpleChannelInboundHandler; import io.netty.channel.nio.NioIoHandler; import io.netty.channel.socket.SocketChannel; import io.netty.channel.socket.nio.NioServerSocketChannel; import io.netty.handler.codec.LineBasedFrameDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringEncoder; import java.io.BufferedReader; import java.io.InputStreamReader; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.net.Socket; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8; /** One event loop. Client A asks for SLOW (a 1 s call to the back office); client B asks for FAST 50 ms later. */ public class BlockingLoopDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { run(false); run(true); } static String work(String line) throws InterruptedException { if (line.equals("SLOW")) Thread.sleep(1_000); // stands in for a slow blocking call, such as a database query return line + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName(); } static void run(boolean dispatch) throws Exception { EventLoopGroup group = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); ExecutorService blockingPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, r -> new Thread(r, "back-office")); try { Channel server = new ServerBootstrap().group(group).channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class) .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { @Override protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) { ch.pipeline().addLast(new LineBasedFrameDecoder(1024), new StringDecoder(UTF_8), new StringEncoder(UTF_8), new SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>() { @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) throws Exception { if (!dispatch) { ctx.writeAndFlush(work(line) + "\n"); // blocks the event loop return; } blockingPool.execute(() -> { // leave the loop for the slow part String reply; try { reply = work(line); } catch (InterruptedException e) { reply = "interrupted"; } ctx.writeAndFlush(reply + "\n"); // safe from any thread }); } }); } }) .bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0).sync().channel(); int port = ((InetSocketAddress) server.localAddress()).getPort(); try (Socket a = new Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port); Socket b = new Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port)) { BufferedReader aIn = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(a.getInputStream(), UTF_8)); BufferedReader bIn = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(b.getInputStream(), UTF_8)); a.getOutputStream().write("SLOW\n".getBytes(UTF_8)); Thread.sleep(50); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); b.getOutputStream().write("FAST\n".getBytes(UTF_8)); // lag probe: how long until a trivial task runs on the loop? long lagMs = group.next().submit(() -> (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000).get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); String fast = bIn.readLine(); long fastMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.println(dispatch ? "[dispatch to the back office]" : "[blocking in the handler]"); System.out.printf(" event-loop lag probe: %d ms%n", lagMs); System.out.printf(" FAST reply after %d ms: %s%n", fastMs, fast); System.out.printf(" SLOW reply: %s%n", aIn.readLine()); } server.close().sync(); } finally { group.shutdownGracefully(0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync(); // close channels and loops first... blockingPool.shutdown(); // ...then the pool they write from } } }

Client A asks for SLOW (a 1 s call to the back office); client B asks for FAST 50 ms later. */ fun main() { runLoop(dispatch = false) runLoop(dispatch = true) } private fun slowWork(line: String): String { if (line == "SLOW") Thread.sleep(1_000) // stands in for a slow blocking call, such as a database query return "$line on ${Thread.currentThread().name}" } private fun runLoop(dispatch: Boolean) { val group = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()) val blockingPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4) { r -> Thread(r, "back-office") } try { val server = ServerBootstrap().group(group).channel(NioServerSocketChannel::class.java) .childHandler(object : ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { override fun initChannel(ch: SocketChannel) { ch.pipeline().addLast(LineBasedFrameDecoder(1024), StringDecoder(UTF_8), StringEncoder(UTF_8), object : SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>() { override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { if (!dispatch) { ctx.writeAndFlush(slowWork(line) + "\n") // blocks the event loop return } blockingPool.execute { // leave the loop for the slow part ctx.writeAndFlush(slowWork(line) + "\n") // safe from any thread } } }) } }) .bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0).sync().channel() val port = (server.localAddress() as InetSocketAddress).port Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port).use { a -> Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port).use { b -> val aIn = a.getInputStream().bufferedReader(UTF_8) val bIn = b.getInputStream().bufferedReader(UTF_8) a.getOutputStream().write("SLOW\n".toByteArray(UTF_8)) Thread.sleep(50) val t0 = System.nanoTime() b.getOutputStream().write("FAST\n".toByteArray(UTF_8)) // lag probe: how long until a trivial task runs on the loop? val lagMs = group.next().submit(Callable { (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 }).get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) val fast = bIn.readLine() val fastMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println(if (dispatch) "[dispatch to the back office]" else "[blocking in the handler]") println(" event-loop lag probe: $lagMs ms") println(" FAST reply after $fastMs ms: $fast") println(" SLOW reply: ${aIn.readLine()}") } } server.close().sync() } finally { group.shutdownGracefully(0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync() // close channels and loops first... blockingPool.shutdown() // ...then the pool they write from } }

try.expect: Blocking: both the probe and the FAST reply wait about a second (995 and 996 ms in one run, 1,005 and 1,006 ms for the Kotlin twin), and every reply comes from the event-loop thread. Dispatch: the probe reads 0 to a few ms, FAST answers in a few ms, and both replies come from back-office. The work is the same; only the thread that waits changed.

sections.html:
Netty 4.2 changed a few things that 4.1 code and older blog posts get wrong.

The default allocator, the part that hands out buffers, is new. ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT is now an AdaptiveByteBufAllocator, and a plain buffer(16) comes back as a direct AdaptiveByteBuf. The migration guide says most workloads should see less memory use, and that it was designed to work well with virtual threads. -Dio.netty.allocator.type=pooled brings back the old pooled allocator if you need it. Lesson 4 looks inside these buffers.

io_uring, a newer Linux interface for IO that lesson 8 compares with epoll, graduated from Netty's incubator to a full transport. Its package is now io.netty.channel.uring, its classes start with IoUring, and you use it like the others: MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup with IoUringIoHandler.newFactory() and the IoUring channel classes.

TLS clients (TLS is the encryption behind https) now check by default that the server's certificate matches its host name. A test that connected to a server with a mismatched certificate will start failing its handshake.

The netty-codec module was split into smaller ones, and the minimum Java version is now 8. And Netty 4.1 and 4.2 can't share a classpath. That one matters in practice. Vert.x 5.2.3 pins Netty 4.2.20.Final, so a library that drags Netty 4.1 jars in next to it fails at run time in confusing ways, instead of with a clear version conflict. Check ./gradlew dependencies for mixed io.netty versions before you debug anything else.

What didn't change is the part this lesson is about. A channel still belongs to one loop, handlers still run on it, and blocking it is still the most common way to make a Netty server slow.

try.title: Switch the transport
steps: In EventLoopDemo, change both groups to EpollIoHandler.newFactory() and the channel class to EpollServerSocketChannel.class (on macOS use KQueueIoHandler and KQueueServerSocketChannel). Run it. Predict first: do the thread names or the turn-taking change?
Now put the channel class back to NioServerSocketChannel.class but keep the epoll (or kqueue) factory. Predict what happens before you run it.
try.expect: With matching factory and channel class, the output looks the same: same thread names, same turn-taking, because the threading model doesn't depend on the transport. With a mismatch, the bind fails at once with IllegalStateException: incompatible event loop type: io.netty.channel.SingleThreadIoEventLoop: an NIO channel can only register with a loop whose IO handler is NIO. That's why the 4.2 migration guide reminds you to set the channel class as well as the factory.

compare.title: Handing a slow lookup from a Netty handler to the back office

java.title: QuoteHandler.java
java.html: final class QuoteHandler extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String> { private final Executor backOffice; private final Function<String, String> lookup; QuoteHandler(Executor backOffice, Function<String, String> lookup) { this.backOffice = backOffice; this.lookup = lookup; } @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { backOffice.execute(() -> ctx.writeAndFlush(lookup.apply(line) + "\n")); } }

kotlin.title: QuoteHandler.kt
kotlin.html: class QuoteHandler( private val backOffice: Executor, private val lookup: (String) -> String, ) : SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>() { override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { backOffice.execute { ctx.writeAndFlush(lookup(line) + "\n") } } }

compare.note: At run time these are the same class: Netty sees a SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>, and the Kotlin lambda becomes a Runnable through SAM conversion. Kotlin saves the constructor boilerplate and takes a function type where Java needs Function<String, String>. One Kotlin-only temptation is worth naming: calling runBlocking { } inside channelRead0 to use a suspend function. That blocks the event loop just like Thread.sleep. If you want coroutines, launch on a scope with its own dispatcher and call ctx.writeAndFlush from the coroutine. That's the same manual dispatch, with a different back office.

worked.title: Hand off a slow lookup without racing on the handler's state

steps.say: A handler counts the requests it has served on each connection and looks up each price in a price book that takes 120 ms to answer. It blocks the loop. The field served is safe only because one thread touches it.
steps.code: final class PriceHandler extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<PriceRequest> { private int served; // per-connection state @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, PriceRequest req) { Price price = priceBook.lookup(req); // 120 ms, on the event loop served++; ctx.writeAndFlush(price.withNumber(served)); } }

alt.html: class PriceHandler : SimpleChannelInboundHandler<PriceRequest>() { private var served = 0 // per-connection state override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, req: PriceRequest) { val price = priceBook.lookup(req) // 120 ms, on the event loop served++ ctx.writeAndFlush(price.withNumber(served)) } }

steps.say: Moving everything into the back office frees the loop but breaks the counter. Two requests on the same connection can now run on two pool threads at once, and served++ is a read-modify-write race on a plain field.
steps.code: backOffice.execute(() -> { Price price = priceBook.lookup(req); served++; // two pool threads, one field: lost updates ctx.writeAndFlush(price.withNumber(served)); });

alt.html: backOffice.execute { val price = priceBook.lookup(req) served++ // two pool threads, one field: lost updates ctx.writeAndFlush(price.withNumber(served)) }

steps.say: Do only the slow call in the back office, then hop back to the channel's loop for everything that touches the handler's state. The loop is the lock.
steps.code: @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, PriceRequest req) { backOffice.execute(() -> { Price price = priceBook.lookup(req); // 1. wait off the loop ctx.executor().execute(() -> { // 2. back on the channel's loop served++; // 3. confined state, no lock needed ctx.writeAndFlush(price.withNumber(served)); }); }); }

alt.html: override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, req: PriceRequest) { backOffice.execute { val price = priceBook.lookup(req) // 1. wait off the loop ctx.executor().execute { // 2. back on the channel's loop served++ // 3. confined state, no lock needed ctx.writeAndFlush(price.withNumber(served)) } } }

steps.say: One thing the loop no longer gives you is order. Two requests on one connection can finish in either order, so replies can overtake each other. Either give each request a number that the client matches its reply with, or keep one request in flight per connection by turning off auto-read until the reply is written. Lesson 4 shows auto-read.

lab.title: Build the price desk on Netty 4.2 and keep its loop free
steps: Run the tests. All four fail with NotImplementedError. QuoteServer is the price desk: each line in gets a reply line from lookup, a function that may be slow.

Write QuotePipeline.handlers: LineBasedFrameDecoder(MAX_LINE), StringDecoder(UTF_8), StringEncoder(UTF_8), then business. Write UpperCaseHandler.channelRead0, the shout-back desk. The two EmbeddedChannel tests should now pass.

Build QuoteServer as its KDoc describes: a one-thread MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup with NioIoHandler.newFactory(), a ServerBootstrap with NioServerSocketChannel, and a ChannelInitializer that adds QuotePipeline.handlers(QuoteHandler(blocking, lookup)). Run the tests: three pass, and the slow-lookup test reports an event-loop lag near a second.
Fix QuoteHandler: run the lookup on blocking, the lab's back office, and call ctx.writeAndFlush from there. Run the tests until all four pass.
hints: ch.pipeline().addLast(*QuotePipeline.handlers(...)) uses Kotlin's spread operator to pass the array as varargs.
Create a new QuoteHandler inside initChannel. A handler without @Sharable may sit in only one pipeline, and the server has many channels.
bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0) picks a free port; port() reads it back from the channel.
The test's lag probe is server.group.next().submit(Callable { ... }). With one loop in the group, next() is always that loop.

drill.title: Write a Netty 4.2 bootstrap from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write the code that starts a Netty 4.2 echo server on port 9000 with one accepting loop, the default number of worker loops, and a handler that echoes each message back. Which class replaces NioEventLoopGroup, and why doesn't the echo handler release the message?

answer.html: EventLoopGroup boss = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); EventLoopGroup workers = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory()); Channel server = new ServerBootstrap() .group(boss, workers) .channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class) .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { @Override protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) { ch.pipeline().addLast(new ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter() { @Override public void channelRead(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Object msg) { ctx.writeAndFlush(msg); // the write takes ownership and releases it once sent } }); } }) .bind(9000).sync().channel(); // MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup + NioIoHandler.newFactory() replaces NioEventLoopGroup.

alt.html: val boss = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()) val workers = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(NioIoHandler.newFactory()) val server = ServerBootstrap() .group(boss, workers) .channel(NioServerSocketChannel::class.java) .childHandler(object : ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { override fun initChannel(ch: SocketChannel) { ch.pipeline().addLast(object : ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter() { override fun channelRead(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, msg: Any) { ctx.writeAndFlush(msg) // the write takes ownership and releases it once sent } }) } }) .bind(9000).sync().channel() // MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup + NioIoHandler.newFactory() replaces NioEventLoopGroup.

recap: An EventLoop is one thread with a selector and a task queue. A channel is registered with one loop for life, so its handlers never run at the same time.
Netty 4.2 builds groups as new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(n, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); NioEventLoopGroup and its cousins are deprecated. The default size is 2 × cores.
Inbound events flow from head to tail through decoders to your handler. Writes flow toward the head through encoders, starting at the current handler when you use ctx.
EmbeddedChannel runs a pipeline without a socket: writeInbound, readOutbound and finish() make handlers easy to test.
Never block a handler. Hand the slow part to your own pool and call ctx.writeAndFlush from there; the per-handler EventExecutorGroup versions of addLast are deprecated in 4.2.
The limit: Netty can't stop a handler from blocking. The golden rule is yours to keep, and a lag probe is how you check it.

explain.prompt: Explain why a Netty handler that runs a 200 ms database query slows down clients that never send that query, and how you would fix it in Netty 4.2.
explain.answer: Each channel is registered with one event loop for its whole life, and a loop is a single thread that runs the handlers of all its channels, one event at a time. While the handler waits 200 ms for the database, that thread can't read, decode or write for any other channel on the same loop, so their requests queue behind the query. The fix in 4.2 is manual dispatch: in the handler, hand the query to a pool of your own sized for blocking work (or to virtual threads), and call ctx.writeAndFlush with the result from that pool. Netty queues the write back onto the channel's loop. If the code needs the handler's state, hop back with ctx.executor().execute first. The deprecated addLast(EventExecutorGroup, ...) is not the answer any more.

deeper.html:
Two details make manual dispatch work, and both are worth reading in Netty's source.

First, every outbound call checks where it runs. AbstractChannelHandlerContext.write asks executor.inEventLoop(). On the loop, it calls the next handler directly. Off the loop, it wraps the write in a task and puts it in the loop's queue. That's why ctx.writeAndFlush from your pool is safe, and also why it isn't free: each one is a task hand-off and a wake-up of the selector.

Second, the loop takes turns between IO and tasks. A Netty 4.2 loop is a SingleThreadIoEventLoop: it runs the IO handler (select, then process the ready channels), then drains its task queue, then selects again. Tasks from other threads, writes from your pool and timers all share the thread with IO. The 4.2 migration guide mentions hooks that measure how long IO processing and task processing take per loop run, for exactly this kind of tuning.

When you dispatch, think about the order of replies on a connection, as the worked example showed, and about backpressure: if the pool is slower than the requests arrive, its queue grows without limit unless something stops reading. Lesson 4 covers auto-read and writability, Netty's tools for that.

To catch accidental blocking in tests, Netty ships an integration for BlockHound (Hidden$NettyBlockHoundIntegration in netty-common). BlockHound itself is a separate library, a Java agent that watches method calls. Installed in a test, it throws when code on a Netty event-loop thread calls a known blocking method such as Thread.sleep or a socket read.
